These Singapore Companies Could Benefit from The Fed’s Latest Rate Hike
article:
Just when you thought the rate hikes of 2022 to 2023 were over, persistent inflation and resilient economic data brought them back, with the
Federal Reserve
(Fed) announcing a 25-basis-point increase to a target range of 3.75% to 4%.
With inflation remaining elevated and economic activity expanding at a solid pace – fuelled in part by surging energy costs and large-scale AI-related capital spending, according to market observers – the hike isn’t unexpected.
For Singapore investors, the focus is on how the latest rate hike will affect the Singapore Overnight Rate Average (SORA) – the primary benchmark for local floating-rate loans.
Since SORA directionally mirrors Federal Funds Rate (FFR) movements, with only a short lag of a few months, the impact on businesses is inevitable, though the observable effects could be delayed.
Still, it’s not all doom and gloom.
We check out specific companies that thrive in this heightened
interest rate
environment.
The Big Three Local Banks: Direct Winners of Expanding Margins
For banks, net interest margin (NIM) represents the interest spread between the interest collected from loans and the interest payments on customer deposits.
Hence, when FFR and SORA drive up borrowing costs, floating-rate loans and mortgages reprice upwards faster than fixed deposit interest rates, swelling the interest spread and thus supporting NIM.
To be sure, all
three banks
saw NIM compress by 17 to 25 basis points year on year in the first half of 2026, reflecting the effects of the previous easing cycle.
But the latest rate hike could help arrest — and eventually reverse — that decline as floating-rate loans begin repricing higher.
The implications?
Even with their premium
valuations
, especially for
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05) and
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), all three banks, including
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), could still enrich shareholders even further.
Notably, with the banks’ direct positive exposure to rising interest rates that bump up core operating profits, this could fundamentally support further price appreciation and/or greater dividend payouts.
Crucially, while NIM is a bread-and-butter revenue stream for all the local banks, they are not dependent on it.
The banks also earn significant revenue from wealth management services and their regional expansions across ASEAN, giving them a diversified set of revenue streams.
Even before the latest rate hikes, their balance sheets are robust – less than 2% non-performing loans (NPLs) and a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio above the required 6.5%.
However, despite rising net profits supporting their extraordinary price appreciation, especially over the last two years, the banking trio’s trailing dividend yields are now 4.1% or less, making these yields less attractive than what many REITs can offer.
S-REITs – Identify Potential Hedged Winners and Vulnerable Losers
Real estate investment trusts (REITs)
are highly leveraged and susceptible to the recent interest rate hikes.
Despite the headwinds, smart investors resist the knee-jerk reactions of panic selling and seek to understand the nuances.
Specifically, the type of debt the REIT holds matters.
So do their operational fundamentals and balance sheet strengths.
To this end, a few REITs stand out as potential winners and losers:

For example, with a relatively low leverage of less than 40% and ICR of 3.5x or more, CICT, MIT, and CLAR could be potential winners.
Crucially, more than 70% of their borrowings are on fixed interest rates, meaning only a small portion of their loans are exposed to the surge in floating-rate interest rates, insulating the REITs from immediate rate hikes.
To sweeten the deal, MIT and CLAR also offer a superior yield of 6.6% and 6.5%, respectively – well above the pack in the list.
In contrast, Suntec REIT looks potentially vulnerable, with its comparatively higher 43.0% leverage, low 2.2x interest coverage and significantly lower fixed-rate borrowings of around 57.0%.
Get Smart: Strengthening Your Portfolio with a Barbell Strategy
Some investors are drawn to the banking trio for the potential NIM recovery that the latest rate hike could bring.
Others prefer the more attractive distribution yields that selected S-REITs are currently offering.
But the two are not mutually exclusive.
On the one hand, the banking trio could see core operating profits improve if the rate hike feeds through to wider lending spreads over the coming quarters.
On the other hand, S-REITs with strong balance sheets offer investors the chance to lock in superior yields while waiting for potential capital gains if the rate cycle eventually reverses.
Rate-driven volatility tends to be temporary, but its duration is hard to predict.
In this environment, investors may want to think carefully before retreating to the sidelines.
Parking funds in cash may feel safe, but inflation can quietly erode purchasing power over time.

title: Elite UK REIT: A sterling case for income, with 9.8% yield and growth
article:
With nearly all of its rental income backed by the UK government, Elite UK REIT is banking on longer leases, lower gearing and selective acquisitions to strengthen its position as an income-focused REIT while opening new avenues for growth.

As at June 30, the REIT owned 148 properties, with 99.4% of its income derived from leases to the UK government. The sovereign is rated Aa3 with a stable outlook by Moody’s and AA- with stable outlooks by both S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings.

Rather than diversifying away from this concentration, Elite UK REIT is leaning into the defensive characteristics of its government-backed income while seeking to extract more value from its portfolio.

In a recent interview with The Edge Singapore, Joshua Liaw, CEO of Elite UK REIT’s manager, says that the manager uses the “five Rs” as a simple framework to guide its priorities: Regear, refinance, reconstitute, reposition and reinvigorate.

“Regear strengthens our lease profile and income visibility while Refinance optimises our capital structure and financing risks. Reconstitute improves portfolio quality and resilience while Reposition unlocks greater value from our assets, and finally, Reinvigorate enhances trading liquidity and broadens our investor base,” says Liaw, adding that initiatives are prioritised based on their urgency, potential impact, probability of success and ease of implementation.

“We want to focus our resources where they can make a meaningful difference to the REIT, rather than expend significant time and effort pursuing outcomes with a low probability of success,” he continues.

One of the most pressing issues was the concentration of leases expiring in 2028. In February, the manager completed the regear of approximately 70% of leases that were due to expire that year.

“This significantly smoothed the REIT’s lease maturity profile, reduced the concentration of expiries in any single financial year and increased our weighted average lease to expiry from approximately two years to approximately seven years,” Liaw adds. He firmly believes the five Rs provide the framework for the manager to address the immediate priorities while pursuing initiatives that have a realistic prospect of execution and value creation.

The improvement to Elite UK REIT’s lease profile has come alongside a stronger financial performance, which Liaw attributes to a combination of active asset and investment management.

For 1HFY2026 ended June 30, Elite UK REIT reported distributable income of GBP10 million ($17.1 million) and distribution per unit (DPU) of 1.55 pence. Both were at three-year highs, with the DPU translating into an annualised distribution yield of 9.8%.

Its portfolio valuation grew 15% to GBP489 million from GBP425 million as at Dec 31, 2025, while weighted average lease to expiry (WALE) increased from around two years to more than seven years.

The REIT was also trading at a 28% discount to its book value, compared with the S-REIT sector’s average discount of 22%. Its balance sheet has strengthened as well. Net gearing ratio stood at 34.6% as at 30 June, compared with its peak in 2023, while the cost of borrowing fell to 4.7%, from 5.2% at end-2023. Some 99% of its total debt was on fixed rates as at June 30.

The REIT also recently secured a GBP50 million sustainability-linked, Shariah-compliant Murabaha facility denominated in sterling, which it says is believed to be the first of its kind in Singapore. “The facility broadens the REIT’s funding sources while retaining sustainability-linked features, including potential interest savings as the energy performance of its portfolio improves,” Liaw says. “Collectively, these initiatives have improved income visibility, extended our lease profile, enhanced portfolio value and created additional avenues for future growth.”

Against this backdrop, Elite UK REIT has delivered a total return of 49.4% since the end of 2023. “Over the past two years, our trading liquidity has also improved, alongside a broader investor register comprising institutional, accredited and other investors, as well as our inclusion in FTSE indices,” Liaw adds.

With its financial position improving, Elite UK REIT is also turning to acquisitions to strengthen and lengthen its income stream. On Aug 6, unitholders approved the acquisition of five UK government-leased properties for GBP31.9 million. The properties had a WALE of 12.7 years as at June 30, and generate annual income of GBP2.6 million.

“The assets complement our existing portfolio of mission-critical government infrastructure,which tends to be less exposed to economic cycles,” says Liaw. To help fund the acquisition, the REIT raised gross proceeds of GBP7.4 million through a private placement. According to the manager, the private placement was oversubscribed, with participation from existing and new institutional investors, long-only funds and high-net-worth individuals.

The acquisition will also introduce His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs as a tenant. Following the transaction, the department is expected to account for about 3.1% of the REIT’s total gross rental income. On a pro forma basis, the acquisition will increase the portfolio valuation by 7% to GBP492.1 million and extend WALE to 7.6 years. DPU is expected to increase by 1.3% to 3.051 pence.

The acquisition will also increase the number of properties with inflation-linked rent reviews. Queensway House (East Kilbride), Challand House (Pontefract) and Bridgend Jobcentre (Bridgend) together account for 61.1% of the acquired properties’ annual rent. Their rents are subject to annually compounded CPI-linked rent reviews, with a floor of 1% and a cap of 5%. This provides “a source of built-in organic growth over time”, Liaw says.

Acquisitions are only one part of the manager’s growth strategy. Elite UK REIT is also looking within the existing portfolio for assets that can be repositioned for alternative uses and potentially higher returns.

One such project is Lindsay House in Dundee, where the REIT has secured planning approval to convert the property into a 170-bed purpose-built student accommodation. The conversion is expected to cost GBP19.4 million, with operations targeted to begin before the academic year starting in September 2027. Strip-out works have been completed, and a main contractor has been appointed and has commenced works. Amid the conversion, Lindsay House was valued at GBP2.1 million as at June 30, up 64% from GBP1.28 million as at Dec 31, 2023.

The manager is optimistic about the outlook for the project, pointing to the latest 2026 Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (UCAS) data showing increases in both international and domestic student applications. “The latest 2026 UCAS student application data for the UK also indicates healthy demand, with international and domestic applications increasing by about 7.1% and 5.0% respectively,” Liaw says. “We remain confident in achieving our first-year ramp-up targets, supported by the quality, positioning and overall proposition of Lindsay House.”

The manager is also working to formalise nomination agreements that could help support occupancy. “Based on comparisons with other student accommodation properties in the vicinity, Lindsay House has the potential to achieve a yield on cost of approximately 7%,” Liaw says.

Over time, Elite UK REIT expects the living sector to make a more meaningful contribution to the portfolio, alongside the stable, long-term income generated by properties leased to UK government departments. “Besides Lindsay House, we intend to steadily scale our presence in the sector through larger redevelopment opportunities such as the one at Cambria House in Cardiff,” Liaw adds.

For Liaw, the investment proposition rests on combining the resilience of government-backed rental income with the potential to unlock capital value from the REIT’s existing assets. “The REIT has demonstrated a strong track record of operational and financial improvement, with both distributable income and DPU strengthening since its recapitalisation at the end of 2023,” says Liaw.

The REIT has also sought to broaden its accessibility to Singapore investors, supported by the flexibility of trading in both British pound and the Singapore dollar (SGD). Following the launch of dual-currency trading in March, its SGD-denominated units were included under the Central Provident Fund Investment Scheme — Ordinary Account (CPFIS-OA) from June 9, allowing eligible investors to use their CPF Ordinary Account savings to purchase Elite UK REIT units through its SGD counter on the SGX. The move potentially broadens the REIT’s investor base and supports trading liquidity.

In the future, the Manager expects Elite UK REIT to remain a resilient income and growth platform, underpinned by its government-backed income stream and opportunities to unlock further value from its portfolio.

“Its portfolio is designed to provide investors with a resilient yield over a long investment horizon, while offering the potential to unlock further value from its underlying assets,” says Liaw.

title: CAREIT delivers stellar first-year report card as living sector assets gain investor attention
article:
Nearly a year after Centurion Accommodation REIT (CAREIT) went public, the REIT has delivered a strong first-year performance with its units up 29.5% at $1.14 as at the close of Sept 2, from its IPO price of 88 cents. The REIT’s key attraction for investors is its portfolio of purpose-built worker accommodation (PBWA) and the sponsor’s pipeline.

In CAREIT’s latest results for the 1HFY2026 ended June 30, it outperformed most, if not all, of its prospectus forecasts. The REIT’s 1HFY2026 DPU of 3.499 cents outperformed its forecast of 3.192 cents by 9.6%, while gross revenue and net property income (NPI) outperformed expectations by 5.1% and 4.3% at $108.9 million and $78.4 million respectively.

The report card comes as CAREIT approaches its first anniversary this September, with Singaporean investors now familiar with the asset class that was relatively new to them when the REIT debuted.

When CAREIT listed on the Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) Mainboard on Sept 25, 2025, it became Singapore’s first global living sector REIT, focused on PBWA and purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA). It remains the only one thus far. At its IPO, the REIT had an initial portfolio of 14 assets — comprising five PBWAs in Singapore, one PBSA in Australia and eight PBSAs in the UK — with an appraised value of $1.84 billion. As at June 30, the REIT has 15 operational properties with a portfolio valuation of $2.21 billion after it completed the acquisition of another PBSA in Australia, Epiisod Macquarie Park, in January.

“When we pushed this asset class [PBWA and PBSA] into the market, it was relatively unknown,” says Tony Bin, CEO of the REIT manager. “So we recognised that we had an opportunity to educate the market as a whole and our key investors about this new asset class and its relevance to the Singapore economy.”

During its IPO, CAREIT attracted 16 cornerstone investors, accounting for 35% of the issue. Together with other institutional investors, institutions now account for about 40% of the REIT, which is “quite impressive”, says Bin.

When asked about feedback, he shares that they are “generally pleased” with what they have invested in and the REIT’s unit price performance over the last few months.

The growing familiarity with the asset class comes at an opportune time for CAREIT, particularly on the Singapore side of its portfolio.

CAREIT’s Singapore PBWA portfolio is closely linked to the country’s economic development, says Bin, given that the majority of its PBWA tenants are involved in the island’s construction boom. And if the government’s latest plans are anything to go by, there could be plenty more growth ahead.

At this year’s National Day Rally on Aug 23, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced several new mega projects including the amalgamation of the smaller islands south of Jurong Island, the refresh and transformation of Sentosa and Pulau Brani, as well as an undersea tunnel linking Pulau Tekong to the mainland.

“These projects will require a sizeable workforce over an extended period,” Bin says. “As demand for workers increases, there will also be a corresponding need for suitable, well-managed accommodation. Infrastructure development is an important driver of Singapore’s growth, and PBWAs support the workforce needed to deliver it.”

Several analysts have already noted that CAREIT, through its PBWAs, will stand to benefit from the extended construction upcycle in Singapore. While no specifics were mentioned, the OCBC Group Research team — comprising Selena Ling, Carmen Lee, Andy Wong, Ada Lim and Troy Cheng — noted in an Aug 24 report that the projects are likely to keep development spending elevated for “decades to come”.

“It’s clearly good news to us,” agrees Bin. “We believe these projects will probably arise in the next few years. The Prime Minister’s announcement means that the pipeline of development works will continue to be elevated in the foreseeable future, and because our workers’ accommodation is a derived demand, we expect these works to benefit us.”

“So there is a possibility that there could be a demand for beds,” he continues, noting that some of the workers may be staying onsite, in factory-converted dormitories (FCDs) and so on.

That said, Bin remains confident that CAREIT’s assets will remain top of mind simply because of the standards they keep.

Of CAREIT’s PBWAs, the new blocks at Westlite Mandai and Westlite Toh Guan, as well as Westlite Ubi, which opened in 4Q2024, are fully compliant with the New Dormitory Standards (NDS), which is to be implemented by 2040, according to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).The rest of its portfolio is compliant with prevailing regulatory standards and is expected to achieve compliance with the Interim Dormitory Standards (IDS) and NDS under the Dormitory Transition Scheme (DTS) as and when these standards become applicable.

The other component of CAREIT’s portfolio is its PBSAs, where demand has been affected by visa restrictions and a normalisation of student demand in the UK post Covid-19.

However, not all PBSAs are the same. “You need to appreciate that PBSAs shouldn’t be viewed as uniform across all the owners and locations we’re in,” says Bin. “Each market is different; the performance in each of the cities could be different. It depends on the university, supply, the price point and how actively the asset is managed.”

CAREIT’s PBSA assets in the UK are located in established university cities anchored by Russell Group institutions, namely the University of Manchester, the University of Nottingham, the University of Bristol and the University of Liverpool.

Bin notes that these established university cities attract broad student populations, providing CAREIT’s assets with diversified student catchments. The assets are also largely positioned within the affordable segment, an advantage given that affordability remains an important consideration for students. In addition, the majority of residents across CAREIT’s UK PBSAs are domestic students, providing some resilience against fluctuations in international student demand, he adds.

Another key differentiator: the properties are managed by the REIT’s sponsor, Centurion Corporation, through their property management agreement (PMA). This means there is aligned interest with the sponsor, who have been managing it since day one in 2014, unlike other properties which are managed by a third-party manager. The sponsor’s stake in CAREIT is now 38.1%, following a dividend in specie earlier in the year from its previous holding of 42.9%.

“The years of experience has meant that they [Centurion Corp] really understand the market and they’ve gone through various cycles,” says Bin. “They’re active in their marketing and they look at possibilities of enhancing the assets when opportunities arise.”

Despite these factors, he acknowledges that the REIT is not immune to external drivers such as visa and immigration restrictions.

In Australia, where CAREIT has two PBSAs, the government has announced limits on places in a bid to curb record migration. In 2026, the government has raised the limit on new international student commencements to 295,000, from 270,000 in 2025.

“We understand that this cap was probably brought about by the heavy demand on housing by the domestic population and the pressure on infrastructure,” says Bin. But he believes that education remains an important contributor to the Australian economy, with international students forming a major part of the sector and underpinning demand for student accommodation. According to Universities Australia, the national voice for the country’s 38 universities, international education delivers A$55 billion ($50.12 billion) in export revenue each year and supports around 250,000 jobs.

Organic growth the way to go

Beyond its current portfolio, the REIT is looking at possible asset enhancement initiatives and organic growth, which it will focus on within the next one to two years.

“We’ve been evaluating our current assets and there are opportunities there,” says Bin. “Because they are existing projects — live projects — a lot of work needs to be done on planning and meeting with approvals and so on. These are not greenfield projects where you can just start on a clean slate.”

CAREIT, which has an aggregate leverage of 29.9% as at June 30, has a debt headroom of $380 million based on its internal target of about 40%. About two thirds of the $380 million headroom are in committed facilities, which provide a “good buffer”.

The REIT is also considering different sources of funding — such as debt capital market raising and bonds — in addition to its current bank debt. And, at the “right time”, the REIT may go to its unitholders to conduct an equity fund raising, says Bin.

On inorganic growth, Bin notes that the REIT has a right of first refusal (ROFR) from its sponsor, which recently clinched two PBWA sites in Kranji Close and Lok Yang Way.

Now that the REIT has successfully listed and delivered good results, what’s next?

“We are always looking for ways to improve,” says Bin. “It is about honouring the trust that our investors have placed in us by delivering on our commitments and, where possible, exceeding them. I am glad that, in our first six months, we have not just delivered, but also delivered ahead of forecast.”

The REIT is also conducting a detailed review of its portfolio and exploring opportunities, particularly within its PBWA segment, which contributes about two-thirds of gross revenue. “We hope to share more when we hear from the authorities,” Bin adds.

For the team, it’s also a matter of constantly improving its product. Even before the dormitory regulatory requirements, the REIT’s PBWA offerings have always come with en-suite kitchens, toilets and showers.

Hardware aside, the REIT and its sponsor have also conducted resident engagement since day one and even before some aspects became mandated. This includes organised weekly activities, working with NGOs (non-governmental organisations) and developing a resident ambassador programme, in which selected senior residents provide feedback to management and act as a link to the wider community.

The approach extends beyond the PBWAs, with foreign workers taking part in community initiatives such as National Day decorations and painting and household repair projects for local residents.

For CAREIT, which has always been ahead of the curve, the next step is to anticipate what’s ahead and shape what comes next. “The challenge is how to take it up a notch,” says Bin.

title: OUE REIT moves to close value gap as CEO Han sees ‘exciting inflexion point’ ahead
article:
OUE REIT entered 2026 with stronger momentum, posting a 28.6% y-o-y jump in 1HFY2026 distribution per unit (DPU) and outpacing its S-REIT peers.

After years of growing its portfolio and strengthening its balance sheet through the post-Covid-19 interest rate hike cycle, OUE REIT is entering its next chapter: narrowing its price-to-book (P/B) gap through more active capital stewardship.

This marks the latest stage of OUE REIT’s Value Creation Journey. Having spent 2014 to 2019 building scale and relevance, and 2020 to 2025 optimising its capital and portfolio quality, the REIT unveiled its Phase 3 Value Creation Journey (Phase 3) in January, which focuses on long-term value creation and compounding growth.

As at 30 June, OUE REIT was trading at around 0.6 times P/B, with its net asset value (NAV) per unit at 56 cents compared to its unit price of 35.5 cents. For Han Khim Siew, CEO of the REIT manager, this reflects a gap between the intrinsic value of OUE REIT’s underlying portfolio and its market valuation, making the narrowing of this gap a key objective of its Phase 3 strategy.

“We felt there was a big disconnect between where we think we should be valued at and where the market valued us,” Han says. To him, the valuation gap reflects different waves of market concerns. During Covid-19, hospitality assets were viewed negatively due to international border closures and reduced travel demand. Coming out of the pandemic, attention shifted to concerns over the impact of work-from-home trends on office demand. More recently, the rise of artificial intelligence has introduced fresh questions over how much office space companies may require in future.

Han adds that the path to close the gap is anchored on three key priorities, which are: growing the net property income (NPI) of its existing assets; lowering the cost of debt; and helping the market better recognise the underlying value of its portfolio.

So far, the REIT has made good progress on the first two fronts.

On NPI growth, OUE REIT has been investing in asset enhancement initiatives (AEIs) to lift its properties’ earnings potential. A key example was the $150 million revamp of Mandarin Orchard Singapore. The property reopened as the Hilton Singapore Orchard with 1,080 rooms in 2022. Following the reopening, Han says the Hilton Singapore Orchard — Hilton Group’s largest property in Asia Pacific — has delivered significantly stronger operating performance than the former Mandarin Orchard, reflecting the earnings uplift from the repositioning.

Across its Singapore office portfolio, OUE REIT has also recorded 14 consecutive quarters of positive rental reversions since Covid-19.

To lower the cost of debt, OUE REIT strengthened its balance sheet. After securing an investment-grade credit rating from S&P Global Ratings in 2023, OUE REIT gained access to a wider pool of potential debt investors and longer-tenor funding at more competitive rates. This was reflected in its issuance of $150 million of seven-year green notes at 2.75% in October 2025. OUE REIT’s finance costs also fell by 16.6% y-o-y in 1HFY2026, while its cost of borrowings fell to 3.6% p.a. as at end-June compared to 4.2% p.a. a year ago.

With asset performance improving and financing costs moderating, the remaining task is to translate these gains into stronger market recognition.

For Han, the way to do this is by demonstrating the manager’s ability to read market cycles and maintain a defensive barbell portfolio strategy.

One such example is the divestment of the REIT’s Shanghai commercial property, the 36-storey Grade-A Lippo Plaza, which was sold for RMB1.92 billion or $357.4 million in December 2024.

In early 2024, the manager became “increasingly concerned” about the asset amid the slowing Shanghai office market and significant oversupply, with estimates suggesting that it could take years to be absorbed. At the same time, the building, which was completed in July 1994, had about 20 years left on its land lease.

Rather than wait for the market to recover, OUE REIT decided to exit the building with just a 5% discount to valuation. In comparison, a number of US private equity funds were reportedly trying to sell their buildings at a 30% to 40% discount from their purchase price.

To Han, the Lippo Plaza sale reflected the manager’s foresight to act before market conditions deteriorated further, and the value of owning an asset at a prime location — in this case, Shanghai’s Huaihai Middle Road, which is known for its high-end luxury brand flagship stores.

“We were able to recognise and time the cycle,” he reflects.

The same discipline applies to acquisitions. Han says the manager is speaking to a number of fund managers and asset managers and is building a pipeline of potential opportunities, but it will not chase assets at any price.

Tokyo hotels, for instance, remain attractive to OUE REIT, but Han says the amount of capital chasing the sector makes valuations less attractive.

“There’re a lot of investors who want to buy Tokyo hotels and they’re happy to bid up the price. We don’t want to be in a situation where we need to bid up the price,” he says.

The same discipline also can be seen in OUE REIT’s acquisition of a 19.9% stake in Salesforce Tower in Sydney. The freehold, 55-storey premium-grade commercial building in Sydney’s core central business district was acquired from Mitsubishi Estate for A$195.5 million, or $175.0 million. The acquisition is expected to be DPU-accretive by 0.9% on a pro forma basis.

For OUE REIT, the acquisition was consistent with its strategy of moving away from older assets with declining leaseholds and higher future capital expenditure requirements, towards newer, prime assets that are freehold or have longer leasehold tenures.

“We have been monitoring Salesforce Tower since October 2022. At the time, interest rates in Australia were still low and the office valuations were higher, with prime office assets trading at capitalisation yields of around 4%” recalls Han, adding that a transaction that took place in October 2022, valued Salesforce Tower at A$2.2 billion.

Rather than entering the market when office valuations were elevated, the REIT waited for conditions to become more favourable before moving when an existing shareholder wanted to sell.

When the stake was put up for sale in November 2025, the REIT was able to “move quickly”, supported by cash proceeds from the Lippo Plaza divestment. The acquisition consideration valued Salesforce Tower at A$1.8 billion on a 100% asset basis, at a time when interest rates were elevated, liquidity in the Australian office market was relatively constrained and the Singapore dollar was favourable against the Australian dollar. The acquisition also gives OUE REIT the right of first refusal (ROFR) over the remaining 80.1% stake.

According to Han, the REIT likes Sydney offices for their longer office leases of about five to 10 years, compared with around three years for Singapore offices. The longer leases provide greater visibility over the REIT’s income stream, with fewer tenants coming up for renewal at any one time.

“For us, it’s a wonderful opportunity to establish a presence in the market, through one of the best and newer buildings in Sydney,” says Han.“If you talk to fund managers now, many of them will tell you this is the perfect time now to get into Sydney offices.”

Refining the barbell strategy: Anchoring on high-quality assets and markets

For OUE REIT, scarcity is key. Han believes offices can continue to perform well, but only if they are high-quality assets in prime locations.

He explains: “There will be a bifurcation where the best offices will continue to have full occupancy and positive rent reversion whereas poorer-quality buildings will face higher vacancies and declining rents.” This applies to hospitality and retail assets, which are seeing similar trends globally.

The quality-focused approach is also where the REIT’s barbell strategy comes into play. The strategy is not simply about balancing hospitality, office and retail assets. It is also about diversifying across markets and property cycles. Singapore offices, for instance, have continued to see positive rental reversions, while the Australian office market is at a different stage of the cycle. By owning prime assets in different markets, the REIT believes opportunities and risks can be well balanced across cycles.

This philosophy is also behind its decision to divest Crowne Plaza Changi Airport. While the hotel remains a quality asset, its hotel management agreement is due to expire in 2028, at which point a substantial refurbishment would be required. Given the hotel’s location within Changi Airport, carrying out the refurbishment while keeping the hotel open would be difficult and would likely require floors to be closed progressively over an 18-to-24-month period.

The next asset that could potentially be evaluated for divestment could be the “very iconic” One Raffles Place, which Han views as the best asset in Raffles Place.

Yet, One Raffles Place’s first tower was completed in 1986. As with any mature asset, age and future capital expenditure requirements become important considerations. A new owner could potentially undertake a more extensive redevelopment or repositioning exercise to unlock further value.

For OUE REIT, proceeds from these divestments could either be recycled into higher-return assets or used to pay down debt if suitable acquisition opportunities cannot be found.

“We like assets which are ‘born green’, like Salesforce Tower,” Han says. “A lot of the buildings in Singapore are not born green. They need to be upgraded to be green, which can be expensive because you’re changing chillers, which cost $10 million to $50 million,” says Han. “We’re trying to move away from vintage buildings that will require a lot more investment to get them to become green buildings.”

In Han’s view, this approach will become increasingly important in an environment where inflation and interest rates are expected to remain structurally higher for longer, partly due to geopolitical tensions and higher energy costs.

For OUE REIT, the aim is therefore not to predict every market cycle perfectly, but to make sure its portfolio is well-positioned to withstand them.

With several potential asset sales and acquisitions on the table, 2026 could mark a defining year for OUE REIT’s next phase of growth.

“The REIT has made a meaningful turnaround since 2022 and is now on a stronger footing,” Han says. “We are at an exciting inflexion point. As we step up capital recycling and focus on disciplined execution to unlock value, we expect to further strengthen our portfolio, continue lowering our cost of debt, drive the performance of our existing assets and improve the NPI. We expect these efforts to support a progressive narrowing of P/B discount over time. This is a multi-year journey, but we are confident in our direction.”

title: Editor's Note
article:
The Singapore market is experiencing a revival following the whole-of-country approach in boosting the local capital market, and the S-REITs should catch up with the rest of the market when global bond market volatility abates.

In a white paper by Eastspring Investments, the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) is deepening liquidity, broadening participation and improving market access. Its white paper shows “how dividend strength, robust corporate governance, an adaptive mindset and a consistent policy framework help shape the Singapore equity market’s resilience, particularly in how it absorbs market shocks through the depth of drawdowns and speed of recoveries. These levers continue to evolve, reinforcing Singapore’s ability to navigate a more uncertain and volatile global environment, and increasing the Singapore equity market’s relevance for investors”.

The EQDP was raised to $6.5 billion following this year’s Budget, to invest in Singapore’s Next 50 stocks. These include 15 REITs, three of which are highlighted in this report: ESR-REIT, Lendlease Global Commercial REIT (LREIT) and Centurion Accommodation REIT (CAREIT). The others are AIMS APAC REIT, CapitaLand Ascott Trust, CapitaLand China Trust, CapitaLand India Trust, CDL Hospitality Trusts, Keppel REIT, NTT DC REIT, ParkwayLife REIT, Sasseur REIT, Starhill Global REIT, Suntec REIT and UI Boustead REIT.

S-REIT performance this year has been impacted, in part, by the volatility of the US bond market. Other geopolitical tensions, including a war of choice by the Trump administration against Iran, are affecting US Treasury yields.

Despite market volatility, REIT managers are delivering on their operations and metrics such as distributions per unit (DPU) and net asset value (NAV). For the REITs highlighted in this report, ESR-REIT’s DPU in 1HFY2026 rose by 2.4% y-o-y to 11.51 cents, while its core DPU, which excludes top-ups, rose by 4.5% y-o-y to 11.25 cents. The top-ups were from gains from properties that were divested ahead of acquisitions and those that underwent asset enhancement initiatives (AEI).

See also: Elite UK REIT: A sterling case for income, with 9.8% yield and growth

Elite UK REIT’s 1HFY2026 DPU rose by 3.3% y-o-y to 1.55 cents due to active asset and capital management; LREIT’s DPU for its FY2026 for the 12 months to end-June rose 3% y-o-y to 3.7 cents as its management focused the portfolio on Singapore through active asset recycling. Elsewhere, CAREIT’s DPU of 3.499 cents for its 1HFY2026 was 9.6% above the forecast in its IPO prospectus. Digital Core REITs’ DPU was unchanged for its 1HFY2026 at 1.8 US cents.

The most spectacular gain was a 28.6% y-o-y surge in DPU for 1HFY2026 for OUE REIT. This was through a combination of a renewed Singapore focus and lower interest expense. OUE REIT’s manager believes that the AUD is cheap relative to the SGD and it’s an opportune time to acquire a stake in a Grade A building in the heart of Sydney’s core CBD. Hence, OUE REIT has invested in a 19.9% share of Salesforce Tower.

The Mapletree REITs have turned the corner, as evidenced by gains in their quarterly DPUs. For instance, Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust’s (MPACT) 1QFY2026/2027 for the three months to end-June rose by 3.2% q-o-q to 1.96 cents; Mapletree Industrial Trust’s DPU for its 1QFY2026/2027 rose 0.6% q-o-q to 3.11 cents while Mapletree Logistics Trust’s DPU rose by 0.2% y-o-y to 1.816 cents for the same period.

See also: CAREIT delivers stellar first-year report card as living sector assets gain investor attention

As investors and fund managers mull over what to invest in within Singapore’s Next 50 stocks, we would like to highlight that S-REITs are mainly delivering on what they are designed to do, providing stable income and yield. Investors looking for yield may want to reconsider S-REITs. Thank you for staying with us on this journey.
